reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: planned concessions under stress, money record never sacrificed, gaps in public provider evidence
Larkfield's two renewal incidents: a delayed run in October versus double charges in November
Part VIII moves from single-payment mechanics to operating conditions, where lateness costs less than error
Part thesis: scale is run by choosing ahead what yields, never the money record (author's reading of providers)
Limits of public evidence on provider regions and failover; uptime numbers cannot compare them
Roadmap of the five chapters, each naming what yields and starting from a Larkfield case
Reliability chapter preview: staying up by letting other things yield, unknown-outcome payments, outage drill
Data-stores chapter preview: sharded databases without cross-shard transactions and the outbox pattern at Larkfield
Residency chapter preview: localization laws versus hosting choices, sparse provider disclosure, customer questionnaire
Peak-load chapter preview: per-account rate limits mean the merchant paces its own renewal wave
Safe-change chapter preview: gradual rollouts at providers and Larkfield, change done when records agree
Reading order guidance and closing callback to late-before-wrong, pointing to the reliability chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All eleven outline summaries match the controlling ideas of their aligned spec paragraphs p01-p11 in spec order (two runs late/wrong; reversal of priorities; what gives way and the record not relaxed; limits of public evidence; roadmap; five chapter previews; reading order and callback). The KEY POINTS callout matches no spec paragraph, as expected.
The outliner marked no unit as carrying two ideas; each unit summarised in one phrase.

Introduction paragraphs carry the part thesis (two runs as the late/wrong contrast, the claim, the evidence limit, the roadmap); the five chapter paragraphs map one to one onto P8-1 to P8-5; the conclusion returns to the claim. No orphan unit.

Figure 1's caption and the closing line of ¶1 ('The first month was late. The second was wrong.') say what the two runs show, and ¶2 draws the cost contrast; Figure 2's caption names the five springs and the unmoved record. Provider facts in the chapter paragraphs are each followed by the point they make (e.g. 'So the party that creates the load paces it'; 'which no uptime figure reports').

p01->p02 (contrast): 'That is not the order most engineers would give them' sets the two months against the downtime habit and carries over Parts II-VII; the referent ambiguity is recorded under flow_is_followable.
p02->p03 (cause_effect): 'So the part's claim is about what is given up' draws the consequence of the reversed priorities.
p03->p04 (contrast): 'That reading has less to stand on here than anywhere in the book' picks up the claim as a reading of published designs and turns to what is not published.
p04->p05 (sequence): 'Each of the five chapters names what gives way so that the record does not' carries the claim forward into the five questions in order and the Larkfield openings.

p05->chapters section (elaboration, end_of_previous): p05 ends on the five questions, and the section expands each with the question in bold, what gives way, the providers' records and the Larkfield case.

p06->p07 (cause_effect): 'follows from that split between the path that answers and the record that must be right' picks up chapter 37's split and states the consequence; both flow readers found it convincing.
p07->p08 (contrast): 'turns from data divided by engineers to data divided by law' expresses the declared contrast with the shards of chapter 38.

results.quote: takes that hosting difference to the day load arrives at once
results.finding: The declared cause_effect is named but not expressed: nothing in the paragraph uses the hosting difference (rented AWS capacity vs owned data centers); it moves straight to per-account limits. The prose needs to say that, whichever hosting model, a merchant meets its per-customer share first. Both flow readers reported this bridge as unsupported (flow-A item 14; flow-B section 2).

results.quote: takes up the problem the peak leaves open, a system that cannot be stopped
results.finding: The declared problem_solution relies on 'a payment system cannot be stopped for its peaks' as known from the previous paragraph, but ¶4 never says so; the problem is asserted rather than picked up. Both flow readers reported it (flow-A item 16; flow-B section 2).

chapters->conclusion (conclusion_summary): 'The chapters run from what must hold ... to what threatens it' summarises the five chapters and turns to how to read them; the mismatch of that stated principle with the actual order is recorded under flow_is_followable.

results.quote: That is not the order most engineers would give them.
results.finding: Directly after 'The first month was late. The second was wrong.', 'the order' reads as a sequence in time and 'them' has no clear referent; both readers only understood it as a ranking of the two failures at the end of the paragraph.

results.quote: Parts II to VII described each mechanism for one payment at a time ending in [[part-7]] with the account model.
results.finding: The book recap interrupts the late-vs-wrong argument between its opening and 'Engineers usually count the cost of failure in minutes of downtime', so the reader has to go back to reconnect them; a missing comma before 'ending' adds a re-read. Both readers suggest moving the recap.

results.quote: Larkfield's October was the fourth of these, met without a plan: a burst that had to wait.
results.finding: Readers had to count back through the list to find 'the fourth', and the page never says that November was the record itself giving way, which is the contrast the claim turns on.

results.quote: the published figures measure five different things and cannot rank the two.
results.finding: The five things are not named, and 'five' collides with the five things that give way named just before, so both readers briefly linked them.

results.quote: Each of the five chapters names what gives way so that the record does not and opens on a case at Larkfield
results.finding: The roadmap paragraph lists the five chapter questions that the next section repeats almost word for word in bold, so both readers read it as a duplicate rather than a step. The spec keeps p05 deliberately (changelog: style guide and AC-1), so the repetition comes from the declared structure.

results.quote: Stripe scaled a document database to more than 2,000 shards (2024) and Adyen a relational one, PostgreSQL, with accounting clusters filled in rotation (2021) (a shard is one database holding a slice of the data). In what either has published, no transaction spans them.
results.finding: The shard gloss arrives after the term, two parentheses deep, 'accounting clusters filled in rotation' is unexplained, and 'them' could be shards, clusters or the two databases; the link to the 'system-wide transaction' that gives way is left to the reader.

results.quote: Larkfield builds one after 146 purchases *(illustrative)* were paid and never activated.
results.finding: Only this Larkfield figure is marked illustrative while the others (7,900, 1,840, €71,300) are not, and both readers stopped to ask whether it differs in kind.
The sentence does not say what the law (or, next, hosting) decides; both readers had to infer 'where data lives' from the chapter question.

results.quote: takes that hosting difference to the day load arrives at once
results.finding: The link sentence promises a connection to hosting that the paragraph never makes, so the reason the peak chapter sits fourth is unclear.

results.quote: takes up the problem the peak leaves open, a system that cannot be stopped
results.finding: The peak paragraph as written does not leave this problem open, so the reason the safe-change chapter comes last reads as asserted.

results.quote: an identifier stop at a border
results.finding: The KEY POINTS and p03 name five things that give way, one per chapter (and Figure 2 draws them), but the chapter paragraphs do not name them in the same words: the residency paragraph never mentions the identifier, and the safe-change paragraph does not name the reach of a rollout as what gives way, so readers cannot map the five springs onto the five chapters and never learn what identifier stops.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, items 2 and 19 (flow-A item 1 and section 4)

results.quote: The chapters run from what must hold, the record, to what threatens it: growth, law, load and change.
results.finding: Both readers worked out the actual order (failure, growth, law, peak, change) and found that this stated principle contradicts it: the first chapter is about failure, not the record, failure is missing from the threats, and the next sentence returns to the failure-first framing. The sentence is the spec's own synthesis and flow rationale wording, so the declared principle needs restating.

results.quote: made by accident in 2026 and on purpose under Keel
results.finding: In 2026 the November run was wrong, not late, so calling 2026 an accidental choice of 'late before wrong' confused the reader; the sentence does not say it means October's lateness. Reported by one reader only (minor).

results.quote: a payment may be late and may not be recorded twice or lost
results.finding: 'May not' can be read as 'might not be' rather than 'must not be'; one reader had to re-read the central line of the key points. Reported by one reader only (minor).

results.quote: Neither has published a cell design
results.finding: 'Cell design' is jargon outside the audience's already_knows list, is never glossed and is used once; both flow readers reported it unexplained.

results.quote: Adyen described in 2021 an edge that keeps answering while accounting runs behind
results.finding: 'Edge' (the part of the system that answers requests) is not in already_knows and is not glossed; both flow readers reported it.

The does_not_know terms are glossed or only named as the spec allows: outbox ('a table that stores a state change and the message announcing it in one local transaction'), localization law ('one that fixes the country where data is stored'), idempotency key and dunning glossed in ¶1; shards and Keel are in already_knows (Keel is also glossed as 'its 2027 repair program').
The page opens on a concrete, numbered example (the October and November runs) and moves to a disputable claim; none of the weak patterns.
'Where to Begin' neither opens with 'in conclusion' nor merely restates the thesis; it adds no new subtopic or body evidence and ends on a concrete course of action.

results.quote: Read them in order, or start at the chapter for your operational question.
results.finding: The conclusion has a synthesis (the two runs as one choice, late before wrong), but it does not say why it matters to the reader: the spec's so_what, that faced with an outage, split database, residency question, peak or risky deploy the reader asks first what is allowed to be late, is absent; the paragraph moves from reading advice straight to 'Begin with'.
'By the end of the part the two first-of-month runs read as one choice, late before wrong' returns to the October and November runs of p01, as callback.to requires.

The intro reader predicted the claim (decide in advance what gives way; the record is never on the list), the evidence-limits paragraph, the roadmap and the five chapters in the right order with their subjects, the evidence kinds (Larkfield, Stripe and Adyen accounts, flagged authorial reading) and the sober declarative tone. Its uncertainties (chapter boundaries such as webhooks, which give-way November maps to) are minor.

The cold reader stated the claim (something gives way, decided in advance; the record of money never does; late is cheaper than wrong) and named the five chapters in order: reliability and outages, data stores and consistency, multi-region and residency ('short because little is public'), peak load, safe change. This matches the expected answer in full.

¶1 opens on the 1 October 2026 run (7,900 renewals a day late) and the 1 November 2026 run (1,840 charged twice, €71,300 refunded, 212 disputes) and ends 'The first month was late. The second was wrong.'

¶4, before the chapter section, says 'Neither has published a cell design, the topology or timing of a failover between regions or which data is replicated synchronously, or how its webhook sender is built', covering all four items, with the webhook item linked to its owning chapter.
